lemma_6.statement: Let R be a ring, let d be a nonnegative integer, and let I^0,...,I^{d+1} be two-sided ideals of R such that I^0=R, I^{d+1}=0, and I^p I^q⊂I^{p+q} whenever p+q≤d+1. Then for every x∈I^1, x^{d+1}=0.
lemma_6.proof: We prove by induction on n that x^n lies in I^n for every integer n with 1 <= n <= d+1. The base case n=1 is immediate: by hypothesis x in I^1, so x^1 = x in I^1. Now assume that for some n with 1 <= n <= d we have x^n in I^n. Since x in I^1, the element x^{n+1} = x^n x is a product of an element of I^n and an element of I^1, hence it belongs to the product I^n I^1. The hypothesis applies with p = n and q = 1 because n + 1 <= d + 1, and gives I^n I^1 subset I^{n+1}. Therefore x^{n+1} in I^{n+1}. This completes the induction step. In particular, taking n = d+1, we obtain x^{d+1} in I^{d+1}. But I^{d+1} = 0 by assumption, so x^{d+1} = 0. The edge case d = 0 is also covered: then I^1 = 0, so any x in I^1 is 0 and x^{1} = 0. Thus for every x in I^1, x^{d+1} = 0.

lemma_14.statement: Let X/k be a smooth projective variety of dimension d, let L/k be a field extension, and put K = ker(CH^d(X x X) -> CH^d(X_L x X_L)). Let p_{12}, p_{23}: X^3 -> X x X be the projections. If alpha and beta are in K, then the product of p_{12}^* alpha and p_{23}^* beta lies in ker(CH^{2d}(X^3) -> CH^{2d}(X_L^3)).
lemma_14.proof: Let b_1: X_L -> X be the base change morphism, and write b_i: (X_L)^i -> X^i for the i-th power. Let p_{12,L}: (X_L)^3 -> (X_L)^2 and p_{23,L}: (X_L)^3 -> (X_L)^2 be the base changes of p_{12} and p_{23}. The map whose kernel is to be considered is b_3^*: CH^{2d}(X^3) -> CH^{2d}((X_L)^3). We use the following basic properties of Chow groups with integral coefficients: if f is flat, then f^* is defined and preserves codimension; if f and g are flat, then (f g)^* = g^* f^*; and if Y is smooth, the intersection product makes CH^*(Y) a graded ring, and for any flat morphism f: Z -> Y, the pullback f^* is a graded ring homomorphism. The last property holds because flat inverse images preserve refined intersections and multiplicities. The projections p_{12} and p_{23} are smooth of relative dimension d because X is smooth over k, hence they are flat. The maps b_i are flat because Spec L -> Spec k is flat. The maps p_{12,L} and p_{23,L} are flat as well. Thus p_{12}^* alpha and p_{23}^* beta are well-defined elements of CH^d(X^3), and their intersection product is an element of CH^{2d}(X^3). Since alpha and beta are in K, by definition b_2^* alpha = 0 and b_2^* beta = 0 in CH^d((X_L)^2). First compute b_3^* p_{12}^* alpha. By functoriality of flat pullback, b_3^* p_{12}^* alpha = (p_{12} b_3)^* alpha. The composites p_{12} b_3 and b_2 p_{12,L} from (X_L)^3 to X^2 are equal: both are the projection from the three-fold base change to the first two factors, equivalently they are the two composites in the cartesian square obtained by base changing p_{12} along Spec L -> Spec k. Hence (p_{12} b_3)^* alpha = (b_2 p_{12,L})^* alpha = p_{12,L}^* b_2^* alpha = p_{12,L}^* 0 = 0. The same argument with p_{23} in place of p_{12} gives b_3^* p_{23}^* beta = 0. Now apply the ring homomorphism property to the product on the smooth variety X^3: b_3^*(p_{12}^* alpha * p_{23}^* beta) = (b_3^* p_{12}^* alpha) * (b_3^* p_{23}^* beta) = 0 * 0 = 0 in CH^{2d}((X_L)^3). The codimension is 2d because p_{12}^* alpha and p_{23}^* beta have codimension d and the intersection product of two codimension d cycles on the smooth variety X^3 has codimension 2d. Therefore p_{12}^* alpha * p_{23}^* beta lies in ker(CH^{2d}(X^3) -> CH^{2d}((X_L)^3)).

lemma_15.statement: Let X/k be a smooth projective variety of dimension d, let L/k be a field extension, and let Delta be the diagonal in X x X. Put K = ker(CH^d(X x X) -> CH^d(X_L x X_L)). If alpha is in K and every irreducible component of Supp(alpha) is contained in Delta, then alpha = 0.
lemma_15.proof: Let Y = X x_k X and let f: Y_L = X_L x_k X_L -> Y be the base change morphism. The map in the definition of K is the flat pullback f^*. Write X as a disjoint union of its irreducible components X_1,...,X_r. This is possible because X is smooth over k, hence regular, so its irreducible components are open and closed. The diagonal Delta in Y is the disjoint union of the diagonals Delta_i in X_i x_k X_i, and each Delta_i has dimension d, hence codimension d in Y. (If X is integral, r=1 and Delta_i=Delta.) Let A be a codimension d cycle representing alpha whose support is the support referred to in the statement. Write A = sum_j n_j V_j, where the V_j are the irreducible components of the cycle. Each V_j is an irreducible subvariety of Y of codimension d, hence of dimension d. By hypothesis V_j is contained in Delta. Since Delta is the finite union of the Delta_i and V_j is irreducible, V_j is contained in one Delta_i. Because dim V_j = dim Delta_i = d, we have V_j = Delta_i. Therefore A = sum_i m_i [Delta_i] for some integers m_i. Now we compute the base change. The morphism f is flat of relative dimension 0. For a flat pullback of a cycle, the multiplicity of a component of the scheme theoretic inverse image is the length of the local ring of the inverse image at the generic point of that component. For each i, the inverse image of Delta_i under f is Delta_i x_k L, the diagonal in (X_i)_L x (X_i)_L. Since X_i/k is smooth, (X_i)_L/L is smooth, hence reduced; therefore Delta_i x_k L is reduced. Thus all the lengths are 1, and f^*([Delta_i]) is the cycle [Delta_i,L], meaning the sum of the irreducible components of Delta_i x_k L with multiplicity 1. Consequently f^*(A) = sum_i m_i [Delta_i,L] in CH^d(Y_L). Because alpha is in K, f^*(alpha)=0, so sum_i m_i [Delta_i,L] = 0 in CH^d(Y_L). Let p2: Y_L -> X_L be the second projection. It is proper of relative dimension d, so it induces a pushforward p2_*: CH^d(Y_L) -> CH^0(X_L). Applying p2_* to the zero relation gives sum_i m_i p2_*([Delta_i,L]) = 0. The restriction of p2 to Delta_i,L is the diagonal isomorphism Delta_i,L -> (X_i)_L. Pushforward along an isomorphism carries the fundamental cycle of the source to the fundamental cycle of the target, so p2_*([Delta_i,L]) = [(X_i)_L] in CH^0(X_L), where [(X_i)_L] is the sum of the irreducible components of (X_i)_L with multiplicity 1. Hence sum_i m_i [(X_i)_L] = 0 in CH^0(X_L). By the standard description of codimension zero Chow groups, CH^0(X_L) is the free abelian group on the irreducible components of X_L. Since the X_i are disjoint, the subvarieties (X_i)_L are disjoint, so an irreducible component of X_L lies in exactly one of the (X_i)_L. Therefore the coefficient of any component of (X_i)_L in the above sum is exactly m_i. Because the sum is zero in a free abelian group, every m_i is zero. Thus A = 0 as a cycle, and alpha = 0 in CH^d(X x X).
